title: WPMS/807/1998 of U.P. JAL VIDYUT NIGAM LTD. and ORS Vs TAHIR HASAN and ORS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 1656 of 2008
(Old No. 807 of 1998)
U.P. Jal Vidyut Nigal Ltd. & others ... Petitioners
Vs
Tahir Hasan & others ... Respondents
Mr. Shailendra Singh Chauhan, learned counsel for the petitioners.
Mr. R.C. Arya, Standing Counsel, present for the State of Uttarakhand.
Mr. M.S. Rawat, Advocate holding brief of Mr. D.S. Patni, learned counsel for respondent
Nos. 1 to 4.
Hon'ble Manoj K. Tiwari, J. (Oral)
1. This petition, under Article 227 of the
Constitution of India, is directed against the award dated
29.05.1997 passed by learned Labour Court, Dehradun in
Adjudication Case Nos. 72 of 1996, 73 of 1996, 79 of 1996
and 80 of 1996.
2. This writ petition was filed before Allahabad High
Court, which was transferred to this Court upon State
Reorgsniation pursuant to U.P. Reorganisation Act.
3. During pendency of this petition, respondent No.
3 - Mohd. Galib died and his legal heirs have been
substituted vide order dated 19.02.2018 passed by this
Court.
4. Brief facts of the case are as under:-
 Respondent Nos. 1 to 4 were engaged as Security
Guard (Chaukidar) in Mini & Small Hydro Electric Scheme
of U.P. Jal Vidyut Nigam Ltd. (in short "Jal Vidyut Nigam")
and had been serving in the said capacity for about five
years except respondent No. 1 - Tahir Hasan, who had
completed only about four years of service. Respondent
Nos. 1 to 4 raised an industrial dispute against termination
of their services and the State Government referred the

2
same for adjudication to Labour Court, Dehradun under
Section 4K of U.P. Industrial Disputes Act. Separate
reference orders, in respect of the four workmen were
issued by the competent authority, out of which, reference
order in respect of respondent No. 1 was issued on
12.07.1996, while reference order in respect of respondent
Nos. 2 to 4 was issued on 15.07.1996. Since all reference
orders are couched in similar language, therefore, the
English translation of reference order issued in respect of
respondent No. 1 - Tahir Hasan alone is being extracted
below:-
"Whether termination of services of Tahir Hasan -
Security Guard by the employer w.e.f. 21.06.1995 is
legal and justified? If not, then what
relief/compensation workman is entitled to and with
other particulars?"
5. These four reference orders were registered as
Adjudication Case No. 72 of 1996, 73 of 1996, 79 of 1996
and 80 of 1996 and they were heard and decided together
by learned Labour Court, Dehradun. The workmen filed
their claim statements stating that respondent No. 2 to 4
are serving as Security Guard continuously since
01.10.1990, while respondent No. 1 is continuously serving
as Security Guard since 15.12.1991. It was further
contended that on 21.06.1995, services of the workmen
were terminated without issuing any notice and
retrenchment compensation was also not paid to them. It
was further contended that no enquiry was initiated
against them.

3
6. The employer (petitioner herein) filed written
statement contending that it does not come within the
definition of "Industry", therefore, the reference is bad. It
was further contended by the employer that no cause of
action arose to the workmen on 21.06.1995, as they were
not terminated on the said date. It was further pleaded that
the workmen were engaged from time to time for a fixed
term and their last engagement came to an end only on
30.06.1995, after which they were not engaged any further,
therefore, it was contended by the employer that the case
falls under Section 2 (oo)(bb) of the Industrial Disputes Act,
1947 and it cannot be termed as a "retrenchment". It was
further contended by the employer that although term of
the workmen was going to expire on 30.06.1995, however,
they voluntarily abstained from work w.e.f. 22.06.1995.
7. The workmen, in rejoinder, reiterated that their
services were terminated w.e.f. 21.06.1995 and it was
further stated that notice was given to them on 21.06.1995
and thereafter they were not permitted to discharge duties.
8. Documentary evidence was produced by
employer (petitioner herein), which included FIR lodged
against the workmen (respondents herein) on
17/18.06.1995 and a notice, issued to the workmen on
21.06.1995 and the reply submitted by them (workmen) on
02.07.1995. In the aforesaid notice dated 21.06.1995, it
was alleged that due to negligence of the workmen theft of
electricity cable took place in the night of 17/18.06.1995
and workmen (respondent herein) were called upon to show
cause, as to why their contract of employment be not
terminated.

4
9. Based on the pleadings of the parties, following
three issues were framed by learned Labour Court:-
i) Whether the employer, being a sovereign organ of
the State, does not fall within the definition of
"Industry"?
ii) Whether non-renewal of contract of service of the
workmen had resulted in automatic termination
of their services?
iii) Whether termination of services of the workmen
is punitive?
10. Before learned Labour Court, the employer had
contended that in the night of 17/18.06.1995, a theft of
electricity cable had taken place in the Mini & Small Hydro
Power Scheme, regarding which an FIR was lodged with the
police. It was further contended that based on the said
incident of theft, notices were issued to the workmen on
21.06.1995 and due to these notices, workmen did not
turn up for duty w.e.f. 22.06.1995.
11. Learned Labour Court, after considering the
entire evidence available on record, has returned detailed
finding on these three issues. Regarding issue No. (i), as to
whether the employer falls within the definition of
"Industry", learned Labour Court, after referring to the
judgment rendered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Chief
Conservator of Forests & others Vs Jagannath Maruti
Kondhare reported in (1996) 2 SCC 293 held that
petitioner comes within the meaning of Industry.
12. Regarding issue No. (ii), learned Labour Court
returned the finding that since the workmen had been

5
serving for last several years with the employer, therefore,
not permitting them to serve after 21.06.1995 is violative of
Section 6N of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act.
13. The employer took up the stand before the
Labour Court that termination of services of the workmen
is a result of non-renewal of their contract of employment,
therefore, it would not amount to retrenchment in view of
provision contained in Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Industrial
Disputes Act, 1947.
14. Learned Labour Court has dealt with this aspect
in great detail. It has been held by learned Labour Court
that the contract of employment of the workmen was
extended from time to time, for periods ranging between 3
months to 6 months. Learned Labour Court has further
held that Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Industrial Disputes Act
would not be attracted because engagement of workmen on
contract basis, continuously for 5-6 years, would amount
to unfair labour practice aimed at depriving the workmen
from the protection of Industrial Laws.
15. Learned Labour Court has also relied upon a
judgment rendered by Madhya Pradesh Bank
Karamchari Sangh Vs Syndicate Bank & another
reported in 1996 (1) SCT 199 (M.P) in support of its
finding that discontinuing the engagement of the workmen
w.e.f. 21.06.1995 is violative of Section 6N of the U.P.
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Paragraph 18 of the said
judgment, which summarized the law on the point, is
extracted below:-
"18. From the decisions noted above, it becomes
apparent:-

6
(i) that the provisions of Section 2(oo)(bb) are to be
construed benevolently in favour of the
workman;
(ii) that if the workman is allowed to continue in
service by making periodic appointments from
time to time, then it can be said that the case
would not fall under Section 2(oo)(bb);
(iii) that the provisions of Section 2(oo)(bb) are not to
be interpreted in the manner which may stifle
the main provision;
(iv) that if the workman continues in service, the non
renewal of the contract can be deemed as mala
fide and it may amount to be a fraud on statute;
(v) that there would be strong resumption of non-applicability of Section 2(oo)(bb) where the work
is of continuous nature and there is nothing on
record that the work for which a workman has
been appointed had come to an end."
16. Contention of the employer that the workmen
had voluntarily abstained from work w.e.f. 22.06.1995 has
also been dealt with by learned Labour Court. Learned
Labour Court has disbelieved this contention of the
employer by holding that it is incomprehensible that when
the contract of employment of the workmen was valid upto
30.06.1995, then they voluntarily left the employment few
days before completion of the contract period. Learned
Labour Court has also recorded a finding that the date of
termination, mentioned in the reference order, appears to
be correct, as on 21.06.1995 itself, a show cause notice
was issued to the workmen, regarding theft of electricity
cables, therefore, it was held that termination of services of
the workmen was made w.e.f. 21.06.1995.

7
17. Regarding issue No. (iii), learned Labour Court
recorded a categorical finding that termination of services
of the workmen was punitive in nature, as charge of
negligence was leveled against them by the notice issued on
21.06.1995 and their explanation was called on or before
03.07.1995. It has been further held by learned Labour
Court that the workmen had submitted their explanation
on 02.07.1995 but before that, their services were
terminated. Since no decision on the explanation,
submitted by the workmen, was taken by the employer,
therefore, learned Labour Court recorded a finding that
termination of services of the workmen is by way of
punishment.
18. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that
the findings returned by the Labour Court are
unsustainable. According to him, Jal Vidyut Nigam is
owned and controlled by the State Government and is an
instrumentality of the State, therefore, it is not an
"Industry", as defined under Industrial Disputes Act. He
further submits that petitioner corporation is discharging
sovereign functions of the State, thus it is not amenable to
jurisdiction of Labour Court.
19. Learned Labour Court has repelled the
contention that petitioner is not an industry by referring to
the judgment rendered in Chief Conservator of Forests &
others (supra). I am of the considered opinion that learned
Labour Court was justified in holding that Jal Vidyut Nigam
is an "Industry", for the following reasons:-

8
(i) Power generation is a commercial activity
and a number of private players are engaged in the
generation and distribution of power/electricity.
Merely because some corporations, involved in
generation/distribution of power, are State owned will
not exclude them from the definition of an "Industry".
(ii) Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of
Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board, etc. Vs
R. Rajjapa & others reported in (1978) 2 SCC 213
has defined the term "Industry". In view of that
definition, the contention of the petitioner that it is not
an "Industry" cannot be accepted.
(iii) Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of
Balmer Lawrie & Co. Ltd. & others Vs Partha
Sarathi Sen Roy & others reported in (2013) 8 SCC
345 has considered and discussed the concept of
sovereign functions of the State. Relevant paragraphs
of the said judgment are extracted below:-
"18. Often, there is confusion when the concept
of sovereign functions is extended to include all
welfare activities. However, the court must be very
conscious whilst taking a decision as regards the said
issue, and must take into consideration the nature of
the body's powers and the manner in which they are
exercised. What functions have been approved to be
sovereign are the defence of the country, the raising of
armed forces, making peace or waging war, foreign
affairs, the power to acquire and retain territory, etc.
and the same are not amenable to the jurisdiction of
ordinary civil courts.

9
20. Every governmental function need not be
sovereign. State activities are multifarious. Therefore,
a scheme or a project, sponsoring trading activities
may well be among the State's essential functions,
which contribute towards its welfare activities aimed
at the benefit of its subjects, and such activities can
also be undertaken by private persons, corporates
and companies. Thus, considering the wide
ramifications, sovereign functions should be restricted
to those functions, which are primarily inalienable,
and which can be performed by the State alone. Such
functions may include legislative functions, the
administration of law, eminent domain, maintenance
of law and order, internal and external security, grant
of pardon, etc. Therefore, mere dealing in a subject by
the State, or the monopoly of the State in a particular
field, would not render an enterprise sovereign in
nature."
20. In the case of Agricultural Produce Market
Committee Vs Ashok Harikuni and another Vs Ashok
Harikuni & another reported in (2000) 8 SCC 61 has
also discussed the sovereign functions of the
Government/State. Relevant paragraphs of the said
judgment are extracted below:-
"21. In other words, it all depends on the nature of
power and the manner of its exercise. What is approved to
be "Sovereign" is defence of the country, raising armed
forces, making peace or war, foreign affairs, power to
acquire and retain territory. These are not amenable to the
jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts. The other functions of
the State including welfare activity of State could not be
construed as "sovereign" exercise of power. Hence, every

10
governmental function need not be "sovereign". State
activities are multifarious, from the primal sovereign power,
which exclusively inalienably could be exercised by the
Sovereign alone, which is not subject to challenge in any
civil court to all the welfare activities, which would be
undertaken by any private person. So merely if one is an
employee of statutory bodies would not take it outside the
Central Act. If that be so then Section 2 (a) of the Central
Act read with Schedule I gives large number of statutory
bodies which should have been excluded, which is not.
Even if a statute confers on any statutory body, any
function which could be construed to be "sovereign" in
nature would not mean every other functions under the
same statute to be also sovereign. The court should
examine the statute to severe one from the other by
comprehensively examining various provisions of that
statute. In interpreting any statute to find it is "industry" or
not we have to find its pith and substance. The Central
Act is enacted to maintain harmony between employer and
employee which brings peace and amity in its functioning.
This peace and amity should be the objective in the
functioning of all enterprises. This is to the benefit of both,
employer and employee. Misuse of rights and obligations by
either or stretching it beyond permissible limits have to be
dealt with within the frame work of the law but endeavor
should not be in all circumstances to exclude any enterprise
from its ambit. That is why courts have been defining
"industry" in the widest permissible limits and "sovereign"
functioning within its limited orbit.
23. With reference to Irrigation Department of the
State of Punjab this Court considered the question whether
it is an "industry" within the meaning of Section 2(j) of the

11
Central Act. The function of this Department is for the
development of agriculture. It undertakes harness of the
surface and groundwater resources of the State, the
equitable distribution. It involves construction of major,
medium and minor irrigation projects, maintenance of
network of channels, regulation of canal supplies,
enforcement of water laws etc. It is also responsible to
provide protection to the valuable irrigated lands and public
property from flooding, river action and waterlogging. This
requires construction of flood protection, river training,
drainage and anti-waterlogging works and their
maintenance. Its functions includes plan for irrigation
development in the State. Each of these functions overall
are inherently of the State. With reference to this Irrigation
Department in Des Raj v. State of Punjab (1998 (2) SCC
537) this Court held:-
With regard to the activities of the Irrigation
Department and as also the tests laid down in various
decisions of this Court particularly applying the
Dominant Nature test in Bangalore Water Supply and
Sewerage Board case (Supra), it was held to be an
"industry".
27. It is true various functionaries under this Act are
creatures of statute. But creation as such, by itself, cannot
confer on it the status of performing inalienable functions of
the State. The main controlling functions and power is
conferred on the market committee whose constitution itself
reveals, except one or two, the rest are all elected members
representing some or other class from the public. In fact, all
governmental functions cannot be construed to be either
primary or inalienable sovereign function. Hence even if
some of the functionaries under the State Act could be said
to be performing sovereign functions of the State

12
Government that by itself would not make the dominant
object to be sovereign in nature or take the aforesaid Act
out of the purview of the Central Act.
28. Thus merely an enterprise being statutory
corporation, creature under a statute, would not take it
outside the ambit of "industry" as defined under the Central
Act. We do not find the present case falling under any
exception laid down in the Bangalore Sewerage Board
case. The mere fact that some employees of the appellant
are government servants would make no difference as the
true test to find - has to be gathered from the dominant
object for which functionaries are working. It cannot be
doubted that the appellant is an undertaking performing its
duties in a systematic and organised manner, regulating
the marketing and trading of agricultural produce,
rendering services to the community. In the present case, as
we have recorded earlier, we are concerned only with those
employees who are not government servants. Testing the
dominant object as laid down in Bangalore Sewerage
Board case, we reach to inescapable conclusion that none
of the activities of the Agriculture Produce Market
Committee could be construed to be sovereign in nature.
Hence we have no hesitation to hold that this corporation
falls within the definition of "industry" under Section 2(j) of
the Central Act."
21. Learned counsel for the petitioner further
submits that learned Labour Court committed manifest
error of law in holding that Section 6N of the U.P.
Industrial Act has been violated by ignoring the specific
stand taken by the employer that in view of provision
contained in Section 2 (oo)(bb) of Industrial Disputes Act, it
is not a case of retrenchment. This submission though

13
looks attractive in the first blush, but on deeper scrutiny, it
does not deserve acceptance.
22. Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of U.P. State
Sugar Corporation Ltd. Vs Om Prakash Upadhyay
reported in 2002 (10) SCC 89 has held that provision
contained in Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Industrial Disputes
Act is not attracted to a case covered by U.P. Industrial
Disputes Act.
23. In the present case, reference was made by State
of Uttar Pradesh by invoking Section 4K of the U.P.
Industrial Disputes Act, therefore, in view of the law laid
down in the case of U.P. Sugar Corporation Ltd. (supra),
Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Central Disputes Act will not have
any application. Relevant paragraphs of the said judgment
are extracted below:-
"3. On the application of the State Act or the Central
Act to the case on hand, the High Court followed a Division
Bench ruling in Jai Kishun v. U.P. Coop. Bank Ltd. reported
in 1989 UPLBEC 149 and made it plain that the provisions
of Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Central Industrial Disputes Act
would not apply in respect of proceedings arising under the
U.P. Industrial Disputes Act. The High Court also noticed
the contrary view in this regard in the case of Pushpa
Agarwal v. Regional Inspectors of Girls Schools, Meerut
reported in 1995-II-LLJ-264 (All) but held that in Jai
Kishun's case (supra), the relevant provisions had been
duly considered which are not taken note of in the Pushpa
Agarwal's case (supra) and on that basis, it followed the
decision in Jai Kishun's case (supra). It is this judgment
that is brought in appeal before us in these proceedings.

14
4. The definition of 'retrenchment' under the State
Act is identical to the one available in the Central Act prior
to the amendment by Act 49 of 1984. It is not in dispute
that the law, as applicable then, would be applicable to the
present case if the Central Act is not attracted.
5. The law is settled that under the Central Act
every case of retrenchment would not include a case of
contractual termination which came to be introduced under
the Central Act by Amending Act 49 of 1984 which purports
to exclude from the ambit of the definition of 'retrenchment'
inter alia : (i) termination of service of a workman as a
result of the non-renewal of the contract of employment
between the employer and the workman concerned on its
expiry or (ii) termination of the contract of employment in
terms of a stipulation contained in the contract of
employment in that behalf. Such a case is not available
under the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act. Is the U.P. Industrial
Disputes Act covers the present case then termination of the
services of the respondent would certainly result in
retrenchment while it is not so under the Central Industrial
Disputes Act in view of exceptional clauses referred to
above. While the former situation results in retrenchment,
the latter situation does not amount to retrenchment if the
same case would arise under the State Industrial Disputes
Act. Thus operation of the two enactments would bring to
the forefront the obvious repugnancy between them. In such
a case as to how the question is to be resolved needs to be
considered in the present case.
6. Inasmuch as the enactments, both by the State
and the Centre are under the Concurrent List, we are urged
to look to Article 254(2) of the Constitution of India. If we
view from that angle, U.P. Industrial Disputes Act also
covers the same field as the Central Industrial Disputes Act.

15
However, Section 2(oo)(bb) is obviously a special provision
enacted in order to understand the meaning of
'retrenchment' and that is the law made by Parliament
subsequent to the State enactment and naturally falls
within the proviso to Article 254(2). If that is so, the Central
Act will hold the field because in the State enactment there
is no provision akin to Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Central
Industrial Disputes Act. Therefore, we would have taken
that view but for the special provisions in the Central Act
which we will advert to hereinafter.
7. Section 1(2) of the Central Act provides that the
Act "extends to the whole of India" and this sub-section
was substituted for the original sub-section (2) by the
Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous
Provisions) Act, 1956 (36 of 1956) with effect from August
29, 1956. Under that Act Section 31 (which came into force
from October 7, 1956) has been introduced which reads as
follows :
"31. Act not to over-ride State laws -
(1) If, immediately before the commencement of
this Act, there is in force in any State any Provincial
Act or State Act relating to the settlement or
adjudication of disputes the operation of such an Act
in that State in relation to matters covered by that Act
shall not be affected by the Industrial Disputes Act,
1947, as amended by this Act.
(2) For the removal of doubts it is hereby
declared that nothing in this section shall be deemed
to preclude the Central Government or the National
Tribunal from exercising any powers conferred on it
by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as amended by
this Act"

16
8. Sub-section (1) of the said section makes it clear
that the operation of the State Act will not be affected by
the Central Act. With this legislative history of the law, we
think the High Court is justifies in its view."
24. The contention of the petitioner that services of
the workmen were terminated, due to non-renewal of
contract, is unsustainable in the eyes of law. According to
the own showing of the petitioner, the contract of
employment of workmen was valid upto 30.06.1995 while
their services were discontinued w.e.f. 21.06.1995. Learned
Labour Court has recorded categorical finding that services
of the workmen were terminated due to theft of electricity
cable, as charge of negligence was leveled against them.
Learned Labour Court has recorded finding of fact based
on evidence on record that termination of services of the
workmen was effected on 21.06.1995 and not upon expiry
of the term of contract.
25. In such view of the matter also, defence of non-renewal of contract, taken by the petitioner, is without any
substance.
26. Learned counsel for the petitioner has lastly
submitted that learned Labour Court erred in recording a
finding that termination of services of the workmen was
punitive in nature, while it is a case of termination
simplicitor.
27. Learned Labour Court has considered this aspect
in great detail and held that a notice was issued to the
workmen on 21.06.1995, calling upon them to cause on or
before 03.07.1995. The workmen submitted their reply on

17
02.07.1995, but their services were terminated much
earlier. Learned Labour Court has further observed that
since the workmen had denied the charge of negligence
leveled against them, therefore, no decision was taken on
their reply to the show cause notice.
28. Issuing show cause notice, in which the workmen
were charged with negligence and terminating services of
the workmen on the same day, without waiting for their
reply and not taking any decision on their reply, leaves no
room for doubt that the termination is by way of
punishment.
29. It is settled position in law that before
terminating service of an employee, for a charge or
misconduct, principle of natural justice has to be followed.
In other words, reasonable opportunity of hearing has to be
given to the person concerned, which was not done in the
case at hand. In the present case, services of the workmen
were terminated on the same day when show cause notice
was issued, although time fixed for reply to the show cause
notice was upto 03.07.1995.
30. In view of the aforesaid reasons, this Court does
not find any infirmity in the award given by Labour Court.
Thus, there is no scope for interference with the impugned
award.
31. Even otherwise also, Hon'ble Supreme Court in
the case of Sadhana Lodh Vs National Insurance Co.
Ltd. & another reported in (2003) 3 SCC 524 has held
that the supervisory jurisdiction conferred on the High
Courts under Article 227 of the Constitution is confined only

18
to see whether an inferior court or tribunal has proceeded
within the parameters of its jurisdiction. In the exercise of
its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution, High
Court does not act as an appellate court or tribunal and it is
not open to it to review or reassess the evidence upon which
the inferior court or tribunal has passed an order. The said
judgment has been relied upon by Hon'ble Supreme Court
in the case of Raj Kumar Bhatia Vs Subhash Chander
Bhatia reported in (2018) 2 SCC 87.
32. For the aforesaid reasons, I do not find any
ground to interfere with the impugned award.
Consequently, writ petition fails and is hereby dismissed.
(Manoj K. Tiwari, J.)
08.05.2018
Aswal
